item.title: Does ‘training to failure’ build better muscle strength?
item.description: Stopping shortly before failure can preserve technique and reduce fatigue while providing an effective training stimulus.
item.content:encoded:
It is easy to assume that harder training always produces better results. In resistance training, which includes lifting weights or using resistance machines, taking every set to the point where you cannot complete another repetition may create more fatigue without producing better results.

A repetition, or rep, is one complete movement of an exercise. A set is a group of repetitions performed without a long rest.

Training to failure means continuing a set until you cannot complete another full repetition with acceptable technique, despite making your best effort. This is sometimes called momentary muscular failure.

An alternative is to stop while you could still perform one or more repetitions. This is described as repetitions in reserve, or RIR. If you could complete 10 repetitions but stop after eight, you have two repetitions in reserve, usually written as 2 RIR.

Why might training close to failure help?

Muscles are made up of individual cells called muscle fibres. These fibres are broadly classified as type 1 or type 2 fibres and are controlled by the nervous system. The type 2 fibres produce more force and can grow more than type 1 fibres.

item.title: ‘Toxic’ trailer: Yash in a double role in larger-than-life action thriller by Geethu Mohandas
item.description: The movie also stars Kiara Advani, Nayanthara, Huma Qureshi, Rukmini Vasanth, Tara Sutaria and Akshay Oberoi.
item.content:encoded:
The first full-length trailer of Toxic reveals a world of high stakes, hyper-real visuals and heightened emotions. Directed by Geethu Mohandas (Liar’s Dice, Moothon), Toxic stars and has been co-written by Yash.

The Kannada star has also co-produced the film, which is his second release in 2026 alongside Ramayana: Chapter 1 (in which he plays Raavan). The sprawling cast of Toxic includes Kiara Advani, Rukmini Vasanth, Nayanthara, Tara Sutaria, Huma Qureshi, Darrell D’Silva, Sudev Nair, Akshay Oberoi and Sanjeeda Shaikh.

Yash plays both Raya and his son Rumi, who also goes by the name Ticket. There are hints in the trailer of a father-son conflict that blows up in spectacular fashion.

The backdrops include a circus, snow-laden mountains and a forest. The mood is dark and adult (Yash also appears in a nude scene) with lashings of black humour.

The cinematography is by Rajeev Ravi. The music is by Ravi Basrur and Vishal Mishra. The action choreography is by JJ Perry, a Hollywood stunt coordinator whose credits include the Fast & Furious and John Wick films.

Toxic has been filmed simultaneously in English and Kannada. The film will be released in dubbed versions in Hindi, Telugu, Tamil and Malayalam on August 26.

item.title: Homer’s ‘Odyssey’: Who is Nausicaa, the bold princess who helped Odysseus go home?
item.description: It’s a shame Nausicaa was left out of Nolan’s ‘Odyssey’: she is a good example of how Homer’s Odyssey is ‘a woman’s poem’, as many scholars have recognised.
item.content:encoded:
In Homer’s Odyssey, Nausicaa is a tall, gutsy teenage princess who finds a naked and helpless Odysseus washed up on her shore, gives him her brothers’ clothing, and instructs him on how to appeal to her mother, Queen Arete, for help to get home to Ithaca. She is crucial to his eventual return home after 20 years’ absence.

But she doesn’t appear in Christopher Nolan’s film at all – and her absence is part of a broader debate about how his version reduces or simplifies the role of women in the epic poem. In the Guardian, classicist Emily Hauser mourned the absence of the “delightfully brash princess”, along with nuance and complexity.

“There are more female characters than in most Nolan movies, thanks to the source material,” wrote classics professor Emily Wilson, whose translation of The Odyssey is a critically acclaimed bestseller, this week. “But none of them has much to say, in contrast to the characterisations in the poem.”

This applies to several key characters, from the enchantress Circe, who turned Odysseus’ men into pigs, to Odysseus’ wife Penelope. But what about the absent Nausicaa? Who was she? And why was she important?

item.title: UP: FIR filed against Muslim cleric for allegedly making derogatory remarks on kanwariyas
item.description: The cleric had questioned whether those who assault police personnel or vandalise school vans could be called devotees of the Hindu deity Shiva.
item.content:encoded:
The police in Uttar Pradesh’s Muzaffarnagar district have filed a case against a Muslim cleric for allegedly making derogatory remarks about kanwariyas, PTI reported.

The case has been filed against Sajid Rashidi, the president of the All India Imam Association.

In an interview with IANS, the cleric had questioned whether those who “sit on roads consuming alcohol and intoxicants” could be called devotees of the Hindu deity Shiva.

“Can those who assault police personnel in uniform be called Shiva devotees?” Rashidi had said, referring to a video of a group of kanwariyas assaulting police personnel in Meerut. “Can those who smash the windows of a school van and injure children be called Shiva devotees?”

The cleric, however, clarified that he was not speaking about all those who take part in the annual Kanwar Yatra.

During the Kanwar Yatra, devotees, known as kanwariyas, walk hundreds of kilometres to collect water from the Ganga near Haridwar and carry it back to their home states to offer at temples. The yatra began on July 30 and will end on August 11.

A complaint against Rashidi’s remarks was filed by Narendra Panwar, the chief of a Hindutva organisation named Hindu Sangharsh Samiti.

item.title: In Pakistan, expanding Gwadar port reduces fishers to oil smugglers
item.description: Rapid development in the region has resulted in displacement, flooding and environmental destruction, say locals.
item.content:encoded:
Friday 12 June was a hot day in the south-western Pakistani city of Gwadar. Shamsul Haq Kalmati went to the beach for his usual morning walk but was shocked by something new.

“My friend noticed something wrong and told me to look at the bottom of my shoes. They were covered in oil,” he says. “Looking around, we realised it was not just my shoes.”

The city’s entire coast was coated with dark oil.

Local officials warned the 20 kilometre-long slick posed threats to the local fishing industry and marine life. The threats did not take long to manifest: a sea turtle was soon found dead, half-buried in oily sand.

Government authorities are still trying to ascertain the causes of last month’s spill. Abdul Rahim Baloch, the Gwadar Development Authority’s deputy environment director, says fighting in the Gulf may have caused it. Tankers carrying crude oil are being attacked in the conflict between Iran, the US and Israel. Others suspect the smuggling that carries oil from Iran to Pakistan.

item.title: ‘The Myriad-Minded Man’: A more human, more fragile Rabindranath Tagore in this biography
item.description: Re-reading Krishna Dutta and Andrew Robinson’s biography of Tagore on his 85th death anniversary.
item.content:encoded:
It is Baishe Srabon again, the date on the Bengali calendar when Rabindranath Tagore passed away at the age of 80. On that August day in 1941, the monsoon skies had opened up, yet thousands of people turned up to pay their last respects to Bengal’s greatest creative artist and humanist. Then, the crowd swelled into a mob, and the final procession turned into a grotesque affair. There were stories of a virtual stampede, and people – no one was sure who they were – wild with grief started pulling at the poet’s hair. The result was that Tagore’s own family and loved ones were pushed out. A Tagore worshipper on my mother’s side of the family was amongst the crowd. Determined to offer a pranam, he reached out for the great man’s feet but ended up with a tuft of his silver hair in his palm. Terrified and ashamed, he quickly got away, but most of the crowd carried on lustily.

Tagore’s last journey was, somehow, a culmination of what he had faced throughout his life, admittedly to a lesser degree. The Bard of Bengal had been composing and writing since his early youth. He had no dearth of admirers, but...

item.title: ‘Wonder Tales for a Warming Planet’: A new vocabulary for children to express climate anxiety
item.description: The three stories in the Rajat Chaudhuri’s book cover an admirable amount of ground relating to climate change and its consequences.
item.content:encoded:
I have spent the last five years reading climate fiction for my PhD research – which sounds more glamorous than it is. It means a lot of late nights with dystopian novels, many scribbled margins, and a slowly accumulating awareness that most adult climate fiction, for all its ambition, tends to land in one of two traps: it either drowns the reader in despair, or it resolves the crisis a little too neatly. What it rarely does is leave you with something as simple as hope that feels earned. Which is why Rajat Chaudhuri’s Wonder Tales for a Warming Planet surprised me.

I came to this lucid and compact illustrated collection shortly after submitting my thesis, in that odd, untethered week when you don’t quite know what to do with yourself. I expected something gentle and educational – a children’s book about climate change, illustrated, designed for classrooms and for raising awareness. I wasn’t wrong about any of that. What I didn’t expect was to finish it in one sitting, or to feel, at the end, that I had just read something that understood what climate fiction is and how complex technological usage, like geo-engineering and alternative energy, can be passed on to children...

item.title: Maharashtra CM orders probe into alleged donation thefts at Mumbai’s Siddhivinayak temple
item.description: Maharashtra Navnirman Sena chief Raj Thackeray had alleged that donations worth Rs 18 crore were being embezzled from the shrine annually.
item.content:encoded:
Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis has ordered a detailed inquiry into alleged donation irregularities at Mumbai’s Siddhivinayak temple, PTI quoted an unidentified official as saying on Saturday.

The chief minister has directed officials to examine the temple’s records for the last five years, the official said.

The development came after Maharashtra Navnirman Sena chief Raj Thackeray alleged on August 2 that donations worth Rs 18 crore were being embezzled from the temple every year.

Thackeray claimed that the temple’s weekly donations were below Rs 50 lakh before the alleged theft came to light, but increased to about Rs 1.5 crore after those allegedly involved were caught.

Nine temple employees were arrested in connection with the alleged theft in March, Sada Sarvankar, chairperson of the Siddhivinayak Temple Trust and a leader of the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena, said, according to The Indian Express.

The allegations came amid similar controversies over alleged thefts of donations at other prominent temples, including Badrinath in Uttarakhand and the Ram temple in Uttar Pradesh’s Ayodhya.

item.title: ‘The Tree with Eyes’: Short stories set in Himalayas are horror accounts of ecological destruction
item.description: Bela Negi illustrates the lasting, serious damage done to the hills that usually escapes the tourist’s eyes.
item.content:encoded:
There was a time when writers would escape to the hills, spending their days with trees, streams, and wildlife, seeking inspiration for their art. This romantic notion of the hills is amply felt in literary works born from such circumstances, which in turn, compel the reader to believe that the mountains are sites of pristine beauty and undisturbed peace. Writings across genres – poetry, travelogue, fiction – unanimously agree that there are few things as majestic as a mountain. These literatures have made their impact felt on movies, photography, music, and most strongly, on travel. The hills are the default getaway during the cruel summer in the plains, motorbiking in the treacherous mountains is a niche travelling style of its own, and if these weren’t invasive enough, it is now an aspiration to own houses in the hills, which are increasingly being constructed without any regard for its delicate ecology.

Deep into the hills

Bela Negi’s debut work of fiction, The Tree with Eyes and Other Stories, understands this plight very well. This is the second extension in the state. On July 15, the poll panel had extended the enumeration deadline to August 8 from July 29.

The second extension came after citizens’ rights groups demanded more time, saying that lakhs of persons risked exclusion from the draft rolls, the Deccan Herald reported.

Data shared by the Election Commission showed that only 80.1% of the enumeration forms had been digitised in the state as of Friday. The digitisation rate was lowest in the northern, central and southern areas of the Bengaluru municipal corporation, where it ranged from 49% to 53%.

The digitisation rate was 55.8% in Bengaluru Urban district.

Udupi district recorded the highest rate of form digitisation, at nearly 94%.

item.title: Interview: Why an artist turns to vanishing villages, river ghosts in Assam’s eroding landscape
item.description: Artist-photographer Pallov Saikia believes that art must come from the urgencies of a place and shape a collective voice and practice.
item.content:encoded:
In Upper Assam’s Rahmaria area in Dibrugarh district, the Brahmaputra river is central to people’s lives and imaginations. But since a massive earthquake in the region in 1950, Rahmaria has witnessed widespread river erosion, claiming several forests, paddy fields, villages, and shifting lands in its wake.

There was also rampant militarisation in the early 1990s under the influence of the United Liberation Front of Assam, creating an atmosphere of unsettling silence in Rahmaria. This is the backdrop against which visual artist and photographer Pallov Saikia sets most of his work.

Pallov, 36, works as an Assistant Professor at the Department of Fine Arts and Music, Rajiv Gandhi University in Arunachal Pradesh. He is also co-founder of the Assam-based Anga Art Collective, which has emerged as an important voice from the region.

item.title: Two TISS students denied anticipatory bail for alleged slogans supporting Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam

A Mumbai court on Friday denied anticipatory bail to two students of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences who were booked for allegedly shouting slogans in support of jailed activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, The Indian Express reported.

The students have also been booked for possessing downloaded books and other material that the prosecution alleges reflects Maoist ideology.

Seven others, who were also booked after taking part in an event in October commemorating the death anniversary of former Delhi University professor GN Saibaba, were granted anticipatory bail, the newspaper reported.

Saibaba, who had more than 90% disability and used a wheelchair, spent over seven years in jail on accusations of having links with Maoists. In March 2024, he was acquitted by the Bombay High Court and released. Seven months later, in October 2024, he died of post-operative complications in Hyderabad.

item.title: Harsh Mander: Gurugram’s surrender to majoritarian politics
item.description: Millennium City’s gleaming promise of cosmopolitanism was broken by allowing Hindutva outfits to terrorise Muslim workers offering namaz in public spaces.
item.content:encoded:
Gurgaon over many centuries was little more than a small rural hamlet in the periphery of the towering city of power Delhi. Across the ages possibly its best known resident was Hemu Vikramaditya, a general in the army of Sher Shah Suri who defeated the forces of Humayun and later Akbar. Gurgaon gained some modest standing only as the customary resting place for Akbar’s entourage when they marched to Amber.

Its fortunes altered after Independence. Badly singed by the fires of the Partition riots in 1947-’48, Gurgaon was substantially emptied of its Muslim population. But in the city of wealth and opportunities that Gurgaon metamorphosed into in recent decades, Muslims converged in droves. Yet they still struggle for dignity and rights in a habitat that they still find riven – under its skin-deep glitter – with prejudice and indifference.

Gurgaon began to transform when in the 1970s Maruti Suzuki opened a car manufacturing unit here. General Electrics was the first American company to establish its office here in 1997. Other companies, both Indian and international, followed in throngs.

item.title: August global nonfiction: Six new titles of world histories that deserve a place on your bookshelf
item.description: An examination of the ‘Artificial State’, an account of Queen Elizabeth II and Winston Churchill’s friendship, a remembered history of the Philippines and more.
item.content:encoded:
All information sourced from publishers.

Islands of Forgotten Daughters: Meeting the Matriarchs of Filipino Myth, Carla Montemayor

When Carla Montemayor discovers that her great-great-grandmother was a binukot – a girl sequestered from her family and community, trained to memorise and sing the myths of her people – this sets her on her own epic journey to uncover her ancestry. Why was she raised on European fairytales and Greek myths when the stories of her own people are so rich? And why did no one in her family speak of their illustrious binukot foremother anymore?

Travelling to the Philippines to trace the lives of her female relatives, Montemayor discovers that, officially, her people have no history. Like many indigenous groups, their stories have been erased by colonists. It becomes her work to reconstruct and reimagine them.

Weaving together the tales of her family members, who survived war, oppression, violence, displacement and more, with the myths of her people, Montemayor finds similarities: women with courage, resourcefulness and ambition, who fight and love with equal ferocity.

Islands of Forgotten Daughters celebrates these women and tells their tales, offering a fresh perspective on Filipino history and culture.

item.title: US Senate passes bill to slap 100% tariffs on India, four others for buying Russian oil
item.description: The draft legislation to target Moscow’s energy exports, which Washington says are fuelling the war in Ukraine, received bipartisan support.
item.content:encoded:
The United States Senate on Friday cleared a bill targeting Russia and key buyers of its petroleum products, including India and China.

The draft legislation provides for Washington to impose tariffs of up to 500% on imports from Russia, including gas and oil. It also creates a framework for United States President Donald Trump to impose a 100% tariff on the five main importers of Russian energy, including India and China.

Washington has for long claimed that the purchase of Russian energy has been fuelling Moscow’s war on Ukraine that began in February 2022.

The bill, named after late legislator Lindsey Graham who had spearheaded the draft legislation before he died on July 11, was approved by the Senate by an 86-11 vote.

It will be placed before the House of Representatives. However, the lower chamber of the US Congress is not expected to consider it before September because of the congressional summer recess.

item.title: ‘The Man from Kashmir’: An inventive novella about the unfolding of life inside a collapse
item.description: Mudassir Ramzan’s prose simulates the communal and repetitive participation of oral storytelling.
item.content:encoded:
Mudassir Ramzan’s novella The Man from Kashmir opens with an epigraph from James Joyce’s Ulysses: “History…is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake.”

These lines are spoken by Stephen Dedalus in an uncomfortable conversation with his headmaster, Mr Deasy. Deasy rambles on about his own narrow views – British nationalism, religion, and a grand divine purpose moving history toward a predetermined goal. Stephen counters this view by perceiving history as chaotic, relentless, filled with violence and trauma.

Ramzan’s novella may well be read as the history and becoming of young Dedalus. Ahmed – born in a mosque of the fictional town, Poshmarg, and raised within a particular Kashmiri Muslim texture – dies at the end by suicide in a foreign land. In his prehistory and disintegration are the lives and stories of his tribe that finally weigh him down. When Ahmed’s friend Peter asks Rahil about his profession, he replies:

“What does any brown man with a degree in the humanities do in academia? Colonial studies. Postcolonial literature of India and Africa. He had also been working on a book about Kashmir – specifically, the application of postcolonial theory to the region.”

item.title: Indian court rulings on the ‘right to be forgotten’ will dent our collective memory
item.description: A string of judgements have weaponised the fundamental right to privacy against journalism, databases and search engines.
item.content:encoded:
They say that the first draft of history is written by journalists. This is mostly true, except perhaps in the case of legal history where the first draft is written in the records of the courts by its stenographers and judges. It is these records which capture the present and preserve it for posterity in public and private archives for historians of the future.

As the world moved into the digital age, the information technology revolution promised to make it easier than ever to store, index and organise records. The information revolution also converted much of the internet into an archive which was meticulously indexed by search engines for the common citizen to use for free. So much so that the first draft of history today depends upon the first page of search results displayed by Google’s algorithm.

All of this is at risk today because of a string of judgements tumbling out of the High Courts across India which have weaponised the fundamental right to privacy against journalism, databases and search engines. item.title: Is it worse to eat junk food early in the day?
item.description: The body can process food more efficiently in the morning but blood sugar spikes and hunger pangs can quickly crop up after an unhealthy meal.
item.content:encoded:
Many of us have grown up with the mantra that breakfast is the most important meal of the day.

But whether it’s snatching an extra half hour of sleep, or focusing on getting the kids out of the house, there are various reasons why assembling a healthy breakfast might slip down your list of priorities – especially on a weekday.

So, is it worse to eat unhealthy foods first thing, compared to later in the day? And what about skipping breakfast altogether?

item.title: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye sign defence pact amid conflict in West Asia
item.description: India said that it was ‘closely following’ the agreement.
item.content:encoded:
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on Friday signed a joint defence agreement on Friday, amid the conflict in West Asia.

India said that it was “closely following” the new defence pact.

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, is aimed at “strengthening collective deterrence” and states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be considered an attack against all.

It also seeks to enhance defence cooperation among the three countries and promote peace, security and stability in the region and beyond.

However, the agreement does not specify detailed military commitments or obligations that have been accepted, Reuters reported.

An unidentified Turkish official told the news agency that the pact was “purely defensive in nature” and was not directed against any particular country.

The official added that the pact was open to other regional countries and would not replace existing bilateral or multilateral defence arrangements.

The agreement was signed by Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

It came against the backdrop of heightened tensions in West Asia amid conflict involving Iran, Israel and the United States.

The pact brings together three major Sunni Muslim-majority states: Saudi Arabia, the Gulf’s strongest economy, one of the world’s top oil exporters and home to Islam’s holiest sites, Pakistan, the only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority country and Türkiye, which has North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s second-largest military.

item.title: Nepal’s demolition drive leaves thousands homeless, violates human rights
item.description: The government and armed forces evicted mostly poor and marginalised residents of Kathmandu.
item.content:encoded:
The mass eviction of slums and informal settlements in Nepal’s capital Kathmandu and surrounding districts has displaced an estimated 15,000-20,000 people.

On April 25, the Nepal government began forcibly removing landless residents from the Kathmandu Valley, later extending the drive beyond the capital.

Nepal faces a staggering crisis: more than 3.5 million people are landless or homeless. A government commission invited applications for registration, and 1.2 million people – mostly poor, Dalit, and indigenous – have already registered in the hope of receiving land. Ironically, these communities have borne the brunt of evictions carried out without adequate notice, consultation, or alternative housing. The lack of support has eroded their trust in the state.

The ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party pledged to resolve landlessness within 1,000 days of office. Its 100-point action plan also promised relief to the landless. Yet, despite decades of settlement – some families have been living in Kathmandu’s slums for 60 years – the government demolished homes using the full force of the state. Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, Nepal Army, and the municipal police participated. Residents were harassed, threatened, and even detained before demolitions.

item.title: An evolutionary model that predates Darwin’s natural selection is making a comeback
item.description: Lamarckism contended that an organism may acquire characteristics in response to its environment and pass these on.
item.content:encoded:
Evolution is a fact of life. So much so that even the theory of evolution is evolving. Lately, a centuries-old discredited idea has been making a strong comeback. It helps us explain scientific observations that according to standard evolutionary theory should be impossible.

I’m referring to Lamarckism, named after theoretical proposals from French biologist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1809. Lamarckism stands for the hypothesis that parents of a given organism may acquire or improve certain characteristics during their lifetimes in response to the demands of their environment. And they then somehow transmit those characteristics to their offspring, making those better able to cope with the same demands too.

Lamarck sought to explain why organisms and their environments fit so well together, and how organisms change over time, as observed in the fossil record. Of course, an alternative explanation was provided by Charles Darwin (and others) half a century later. Darwin’s ideas were built around natural selection, which says that some individuals within a species are born with differences that lead them to perform better and therefore reproduce more than others.

The article gave special status to the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir. While abrogating it, the Bharatiya Janata Party-led Union government had also bifurcated the state into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.

item.title: How the BJP stole the month of Sawan
item.description: In India’s Hindutva calendar, there is now only the ‘holy’, ‘sacred’ or ‘auspicious’ month of Shravan.
item.content:encoded:
There was a time when we called the monsoon month of Sawan by its name. In traditional lore, with its arrival, swings would appear in orchards. The air would be filled with the melodies of the kajri folk form and Raag Malhar. The Earth changed its attire as nature draped herself in a green veil.

Sawan meant relief and hope.

For farmers, Sawan is still Sawan. Even today, they call it by that name. Few other lives are bound to rain and drought as intimately as theirs. They await Sawan with particular longing. They know that the rhythm of cultivation changes with it.

Farmers know what the month means for paddy, maize, jowar, chana, black gram, cotton and other crops. Many of their festivals, too, fall in this month. There is Teej. There is Nag Panchami. The agricultural calendar and the Hindu ritual calendar have long lived together.

But we no longer inhabit that older sense of time. We now live within an official Hindutva calendar. It is no longer Sawan that begins but the auspicious month of Shravan. Every mention of Shravan must now be preceded by adjectives such as “holy, sacred or auspicious”.

item.title: Misinformation about health and wellness can be convincing – here is how to spot it
item.description: Claims spread through trusted social networks when people share it because they want to help or warn others.
item.content:encoded:
Recent reports have highlighted AI-generated “doctors” spreading dubious health advice to millions of social media users. Fabricated wellness trends can travel just as quickly. A supposed “pink jelly” weight-loss treatment, for example, reportedly fooled at least one celebrity.

These examples gain credibility in different ways. Influencers can appear familiar and sincere, while AI-generated doctors can look like qualified professionals. Neither familiarity nor the appearance of expertise tells us whether a medical claim is accurate.

Turning to friends and family for health advice is understandable. They may know our circumstances in ways that a healthcare professional cannot during a brief appointment. They can provide emotional support and practical help, and their advice is usually well meant. But somebody can care about us, speak honestly and still be wrong.

Truth and trust

My own research and wider research on digital health misinformation shows that trust can play an important part in deciding which claims people accept. Trust in clinicians and scientific institutions is generally associated with lower susceptibility to false health claims. Misinformation can nevertheless spread through trusted social networks when people share it because they want to help or warn others.

The Reserve Bank of India’s Monetary Policy Committee on Wednesday kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%.

The repo rate is the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks. The Monetary Policy Committee reviews the rate every two months.

The committee had cut the repo rate by 25 basis points from 5.50% in December and kept it unchanged in February, April and June.

A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Basis points are used to describe the percentage change in the value of a financial instrument.

Central banks usually reduce repo rates to stimulate economic growth by making borrowing cheaper for individuals and businesses. This translates to lower equated monthly instalments for borrowers.

On Wednesday, the policy committee said that it had decided to maintain its monetary policy stance as “neutral”.

A neutral stance means that the Reserve Bank remained flexible in adjusting policy rates based on prevailing economic conditions.

State of the economy

The consumer price index inflation increased to 4.4% in June mainly because of higher food and fuel inflation, the Reserve Bank said. item.title: When you hit ‘delete’, what really happens to your data?
item.description: There is a pressing need for provision of concise, accessible and clear information about how deletion really works.
item.content:encoded:
Deletion is a common part of modern life. We send files and folders to the recycle bin all the time, and often get rid of unwanted personal accounts. But do you know what really happens when you hit the “delete” button?

The process of deletion is often poorly explained by tech providers. Lack of transparency around how requests are processed, and the absence of clear confirmation that data has been removed, are frequently highlighted in research.

These issues are not limited to operating systems. On social media platforms and a wide range of subscription services, deletion mechanisms are often just as unclear. Such misconceptions can have serious implications for the wellbeing of users, exposing them to security and privacy vulnerabilities.

A further complication is that many users fear losing data, files, photos and videos through accidental deletion – a condition dubbed “diagraphephobia”. Though this is not a recognised pathology, studies of digital hoarding behaviour show that some people get very anxious at the thought of losing or accidentally deleting personal information such as photos and music.

Such concerns extend the amount of personal data that sits untended but undeleted, ready for potential misappropriation.
